lines.text: You're ninety-five years old, under hot studio lights, and a late-night TV host leans across the desk.
So, Doctor. How many times have you hiccuped?
You open your mouth to answer, and your whole body jumps.
The audience laughs. You've heard that laugh for sixty-seven years. Because you have never, not once, stopped hiccuping.
Over four hundred million hiccups. And counting.
So what if you got the hiccups, and they never went away?
Sounds impossible? It happened. In nineteen twenty-two, an American farmer named Charles Osborne lifted a three-hundred-and-fifty-pound hog, fell, and started to hiccup.
He didn't stop for sixty-eight years. Today, that's you. Only you're a doctor.
Let's go back to where it started. You're twenty-eight, on a night shift in the emergency room.
Your favorite sound in the world is a heartbeat through your stethoscope. Remember that. It matters later.
At four in the morning, a huge patient slides off a stretcher. You catch him. All three hundred and fifty pounds.
Something inside you goes pop. You feel nothing. Then your chest jumps.
You laugh it off. You're a doctor. You know exactly what a hiccup is.
Your diaphragm, the big muscle under your lungs, twitches. Air rushes in, and a flap in your throat slams shut. That's the sound.
Nobody knows for sure why we have them. One theory says it's left over from tadpoles, which close their throats like that to breathe through gills.
Babies even hiccup in the womb, before they ever breathe air.
By morning, the whole shift has a cure for you. Hold your breath. Sugar on a spoon. Drink water upside down.
A nurse pops a paper bag right behind your head.
Nothing works. You go home, fall asleep, and wake up to the same rhythm.
After two days, it gets a medical name. Persistent hiccups. You've written that on patients' charts. Now it's your chart.
After a month, a scarier name. Intractable. It means nothing stops it.
You get a brain scan. A colleague taps the screen, at a tiny spot near the base of your brain.
When you caught that patient, a blood vessel the size of a pin may have burst. Right in the spot that tells hiccups to stop.
Osborne's doctor guessed the very same thing. And just like him, there's nothing anyone can cut out.
So you hiccup. Twenty to forty times a minute. Day and night.
Being a doctor gets weird. You lean in to listen to a patient's heart, and every few seconds, you both jump.
You give up surgery. Nobody wants a scalpel in a hand that jerks forty times a minute.
Eating is like jumping rope with a sandwich. So you blend everything. Breakfast, lunch, steak.
The real Osborne wore out two blenders. You wear out three.
First dates go badly. You lean in for a kiss, and headbutt her.
But one woman doesn't mind. She says your hiccups are like a metronome. Five years later, your "I do" comes out in two pieces.
But none of that is the real problem.
The real problem is the number. Forty a minute is more than fifty thousand a day.
Your ribs ache. Your chest is sore all the time, like a workout that never ends. Osborne said it himself: "I get so sore, jerking all the time."
You fly to the best clinic in the country. A doctor gives you a mix of gases to breathe, and the hiccups stop.
But you can't breathe that gas forever. Fifty hours later, they're back. Osborne's longest break ever was about fifty hours, too.
Then the newspapers find you. Letters pour in. Four thousand of them, each with a cure.
Pickle juice. Peanut butter. Standing on your head. You try them all.
Osborne's friend once fired a shotgun behind his back. Osborne said: "It scared me some, but it didn't scare the hiccups out of me."
In twenty twenty-one, scientists tested a special straw. Ninety-two percent of users said it stopped their hiccups. You're in the other eight.
Hit subscribe if you've ever had hiccups for more than an hour. You're still way behind.
Decades roll past. Your kids grow up to the rhythm. They learn to talk in the gaps between your hiccups.
Your hair goes grey. You're the only doctor in town your patients can hear coming down the hall.
Then, at eighty, your wife gets sick. And this time, you're the one sitting by the hospital bed.
The room is silent, except for the monitor, and you. You keep apologizing for the noise.
She squeezes your hand. "Forty-seven years," she says, "and I never once lost you in a crowd."
You stay with her all night. Hiccup by hiccup.
Fifteen years later, you're on that TV show. Over four hundred million. The audience applauds. You bow, and hiccup.
Then one morning, at ninety-six, you wake up, and something is wrong. The house is too quiet.
You wait. A minute. Ten minutes. An hour. Nothing.
After sixty-eight years, it's just gone. Nobody knows why. Not your doctors. Not you.
And the silence is terrifying. Osborne once said: "I don't know what it would be like not to have them."
You take your old stethoscope out of the drawer, and press it to your own chest.
And for the first time in sixty-eight years, you hear it. Your favorite sound. Just a heartbeat. Nothing else.
The real Charles Osborne's hiccups stopped in nineteen ninety. He died a year later, at ninety-seven.
He was married twice, raised eight kids, and made the Guinness World Records for the longest attack of hiccups ever.
He never found a cure. He just kept living, one hiccup at a time.
So next time you get the hiccups, don't panic. Most stop in a few minutes. And you're only four hundred and thirty million behind.
What's the weirdest hiccup cure you've ever tried? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because next time, the patient is a teenager who stayed awake for eleven days straight.
